Ceuta, Morocco, Understanding the Situation 

For a long time, Islamist rhetoric in Morocco has painted Europe as a kind of promised land, a place where welfare never runs out, chances are everywhere, and prosperity comes easily, with barely any effort required. The objective has always been to weaken trust in Morocco's own institutions and steer young people toward leaving.

But those very currents held power after the 2011 constitutional reforms tied to the Arab Spring. Their time in government produced a sluggish economy, unfulfilled promises, and a public that steadily lost faith. Since then, the pitch has barely changed. The same refrains keep coming back, while Morocco is framed as a failed state, not worth anyone’s loyalty, not worth building, not worth investing in.

In that narrative, Morocco is often branded a kafir state and the King is attacked as not Islamic enough. Young Moroccans are urged toward jihad and a permanent stance of confrontation with the West. Amazigh (Berber) identity, too, is mocked or dismissed as backward, even primitive. Year after year, the effort has been to drain the spirit out of an entire generation, to sell them on one bleak claim above all: their country has no future.

The same ideological current also pushes a claim that Morocco is trying to “reclaim Muslim land” via Ceuta and Melilla. In reality, no Moroccan government has expressed such a demand to the United Nations or any similar international body. Official diplomacy has kept those enclaves separate from Western Sahara, where Rabat has made a formal, explicit sovereignty claim for decades. That difference says a lot about the distance between Morocco’s actual foreign policy and the Islamist storyline built for ideological mobilization.

It’s also worth noting where the loudest demand has come from. A Moroccan Islamist leader has publicly argued that the country “must eventually regain control of Ceuta and Melilla.” By projecting that position onto the state while brushing aside official statements and practice, Islamist activists manufacture a thin appearance of legitimacy for a campaign that aims to weaken state authority, and amplify the message online for global support. Morocco’s ties with Israel and the United States then get turned into a weapon as well, presented as proof that the government itself lacks legitimacy.

Morocco remains a developing country. Real social and economic difficulties persist, and legitimate frustrations deserve to be taken seriously. Still, describing the country as hopeless helps no one, not Moroccans and not anyone interested in meaningful reform. In practice, that narrative mainly benefits two groups: people looking to justify illegal migration, and those trying to strip the Moroccan state of legitimacy.

The timing is also interesting: general elections are set for 23 September, and Islamist operators understand that border chaos, magnified on social media, can destabilize the incumbent narrative before the vote.

Since October 7, this has sharpened, in part because Islamists now face a possible political rival in Fouzi Lekjaa, the highly capable president of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation. Lekjaa is widely credited with driving Morocco’s historic run to the semi-finals in the 2022 World Cup and with turning the national team into a global force. Now he is using his key role in winning and preparing for the 2030 World Cup, co-hosted with Spain and Portugal, to bolster his profile as a potential prime minister, and to deepen his standing as one of the country’s most influential public figures.
 
Contrary to the conspiracy talk that spreads online, Morocco gains nothing from uncontrolled crossings. Some critics point to Algeria’s relationships with European governments, but every major European state keeps channels open with Algiers, Giorgia Meloni’s Italy has a notably strong relationship, while Morocco’s day-to-day cooperation has stayed consistently solid across the board. That includes strong migration frameworks with France and Germany, including a bilateral partnership signed with Berlin in 2024 that has driven higher returns, deportation arrangements with Hungary and Poland, and, most recently, close operational coordination with the United States.

The truth is that Morocco is itself under heavy migration pressure coming from the Sahel. In 2025 alone, authorities intercepted 73,640 attempted irregular crossings, and sub-Saharan nationals now account for nearly 60% of foreign residents.

Last year, several thousand Sudanese and other Sahel-origin migrants also crossed the eastern border, adding to the strain already felt in Moroccan cities, it’s a pressure ordinary Moroccans regularly complain about. The chaos of the past two days only worsens Morocco’s position rather than helping it: once the impression of an open or uncontrolled border spreads, it draws in even more refugees and irregular migrants, piling additional weight onto a burden that is already substantial.

thread_tweets.text:
Morocco is further constrained by Spanish policy choices under Pedro Sánchez. Effective migration management requires reciprocity. The security budget allocated to Ceuta has remained inadequate, particularly with a regional government led by the Partido Popular (whose president, Juan Jesús Vivas, belongs to a party long hostile to Sánchez).

Morocco shoulders the burden of physical presence, patrols, interceptions, and surveillance along the entire land and maritime perimeter. By contrast, Spain’s preventive spending is limited: Spain allocates roughly €60 million per year to measures aimed at preventing irregular arrivals (border technology, Frontex participation, and limited aid to North African partners), while spending more than €1.8 billion annually on reception and support for irregular migrants. A multi-year Spanish government plan of €711 million for Ceuta and Melilla through 2026, covered by El País in 2022, directed the bulk of funds to education, social services, and economic development not pure border security.

This structural imbalance renders Spanish policy unsustainable as it provides more incentives to illegal crossings, not less. Morocco has no legal prerogative to extract individuals once they are inside Spanish territory, including Ceuta. Spanish Supreme Court rulings that have extended asylum protections to certain “swimmers” which were published a few weeks ago only complicate the picture further.

The reality is that 80% of all influencer marketing deals are referral based.

I decline 9/10.

Reason 1: Most products are trash.

Reason 2: As a marketer, I know the effort needed to convince a user to switch to a new product – and this effort is not worth $10 per customer.

Look: I work with many Web3 teams – some are just getting started, others are huge brands sitting at 9-digit FDVs.

I know how acquisition happens and it's never "make 1 post & get 1,000 new activations" – unless you're promoting a waitlist from Vitalik for his new product.

User acquisition is VERY expensive.

I remember the case study @DefiIgnas shared: He was tracking registrations with his ref links and it was not ultra impressive. This is very important because Ignas never posts sponsored content & the level of content trust he has is very high.

For a referral deal to be somewhat rewarding, an influencer needs to be at least a brand ambassador and the product should be very relevant for him.

Because he will need to educate, explain, show how he's using it personally and why he loves it.

If he lies, it will never work.

In this space, everyone wants to "pay for results".
But before you pay for results, you need to pay for awareness and trust.

Let that sink in.

i consider @nvk a friend (even if we frequently disagree on so many things)

i know coldcard was controversial even before yesterday. the losses are tragic and heartbreaking. customers deserved better

i still think it was a fantastic product. i know countless people who took their first steps in self-custody thanks to nvk and coldcard. the cynics will say it was all for nothing but i disagree. and while it doesn’t make the losses any easier to digest, there are also many people who were able to hodl for years thanks to coldcard and did not end up being victims of the attacks.

coldcard was first to innovate many security features that were later adopted by competitors and improved security for everybody. ultimately the devastating nature of cybersecurity is that one mistake erases a decade of strong decisions. coldcard failed where it matters and there’s no way to erase that fact

but i do hope that nvk and the gang, after doing what they can to help remedy the situation as much as possible, and after taking time to regroup, will come back one day and keep on building. bitcoin will be better for it

David Sacks: The Chip Stock Crash is Based on Momentum, NOT Fundamentals

@DavidSacks:

“That is the key question here, this correction in the markets, is it driven by fundamentals or is it driven by momentum?

I think it's driven by momentum. Meaning that over the past year, you've had this roughly 10x run up in memory chip stocks, and you've seen this overall huge rise in any stock that's related to the AI boom.

And I think it was inevitable that you'd see a pullback. I think there was something like a 10% pullback in the Nasdaq from the peak.

But when you look at this momentum trade, it was down like 30% or 40%.

You look at what happened in South Korea, you look at what happened with Leopold's fund, and obviously there was a lot of leverage behind this momentum trade, so when it corrects, it's going to be brutal.

But I think that the question again is, does this reveal anything about the fundamentals?

Is the CapEx that's being invested in the AI boom eventually going to deliver ROI, or is this some sort of bubble?

I think there will be a return on all of this CapEx, and this is temporary market volatility amplified by leverage.”
